analysis.investment_thesis: Gravita is a well-managed recycling business with conservative debt (D/E 0.20) and decent ROE (21.2%), but at 31.7x P/E it is priced for perfection in a commodity-linked industrial business that sits squarely outside my circle of competence. Free cash flow is chronically volatile and reported profits are meaningfully inflated by non-operating other income, making the earnings quality insufficient to justify the premium.
key_strengths: Conservative balance sheet — D/E of 0.20 is well within my <0.3 threshold; borrowings actually fell from ₹548 Cr to ₹445 Cr in FY25 even as equity surged
Solid capital returns — ROE 21.2% and ROCE 21.5% are in my preferred 18-22% range, with operating margin steady around 12%
Revenue compounding — 27.6% 9Y CAGR with consistent expansion, signalling real demand for secondary metal recycling in India
key_risks: Poor FCF quality — Free cash flow was negative in FY22 (−₹61 Cr) and FY24 (−₹56 Cr) despite strong reported profits; OCF dropped to just ₹10 Cr in FY22 and ₹42 Cr in FY24, exposing high working capital intensity of a scrap-based business

Other income massively inflates reported earnings — ₹111 Cr in FY25 vs ₹328 Cr operating income (34% of EBIT); strip it out and true operating earnings are far lower, pushing adjusted P/E well above 50x

Aggressive capital deployment raises execution risk — FY25 investing outflow of ₹864 Cr (vs ₹98–108 Cr in prior years) funded partly by a large equity raise (equity jumped ₹837 Cr → ₹2,260 Cr); rapid scale-ups in recycling capex rarely deliver promised returns
red_flags: Other income of ₹111 Cr (FY25) is 35% of operating income — likely forex/investment gains, not durable business earnings
FY25 equity issuance of ~₹1,400 Cr+ followed immediately by ₹864 Cr investing outflow signals aggressive acquisition/expansion that Damani would find alarming
Business is commodity-linked (lead/aluminium scrap prices) — pricing power is essentially zero and margins are exposed to raw material swings
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Gravita operates in secondary metals recycling — lead, aluminium, and plastic — which is an industrial, commodity-driven business far removed from the consumer-facing, predictable-demand companies I prefer. The core financials are superficially decent: D/E of 0.20 is commendable, ROE clears my 18% floor, and the 9-year revenue CAGR of 27.6% shows real volume growth. But the quality of those earnings is suspect. Other income of ₹88 Cr (FY23), ₹76 Cr (FY24), and ₹111 Cr (FY25) is not operating profit — yet it flows straight to the bottom line and has become structurally embedded in reported net profit of ₹313 Cr. Stripping other income, true operating net profit would be closer to ₹200 Cr, implying a real P/E above 60x at the current price of ₹1,641. That is not a price I would pay for any business, let alone a scrap recycler.

The cash flow track record reinforces my caution. A business earning ₹242 Cr net in FY24 should generate strong free cash flow; instead it printed −₹56 Cr FCF that year, and FY22 was also deeply negative at −₹61 Cr. This kind of persistent divergence between book profits and cash generation — characteristic of working-capital-hungry scrap businesses — is a warning sign I cannot ignore. The FY25 balance sheet explosion (equity ₹837 Cr → ₹2,260 Cr, investing outflow ₹864 Cr) tells me management has raised significant fresh capital and is deploying it at speed. Whether those deployments earn above cost of capital is unknowable today. Promoter at 55.88% is acceptable but not strong, and the valuation at 31.7x historical P/E (23x forward) leaves zero margin of safety for any execution misstep. I would wait for a 40–50% price correction and several years of clean, FCF-backed profit before reconsidering.
